title: When Does Fine-Tuning Extract Stored Knowledge? A Relation-Covering Theory for One-Layer Transformers
claim: The analyzed model is a simple architecture: self-attention with a residual path feeds an MLP of grouped neurons that produces the output.
layout: Single panel, left-to-right, two dashed boxes (Self-Attention, MLP) with fan-out neuron graph
description: A single left-to-right architecture diagram on a white background. 'Input' on the left feeds a dashed gray box labeled 'Self-Attention'. Inside it, the signal passes through a peach W_KQ box, then a light-blue SoftMax box, then a green multiplication node, then a purple summation node. A skip connection loops over the top into the sum node, and a second path goes underneath to the multiplication node. From the sum node, many lines fan out to a second dashed gray box labeled 'MLP'. The MLP box holds three vertical groups of small white neuron circles, with dotted ellipses between them. Each group converges on its own purple summation node. Arrows lead from those nodes to the right, and the middle one is labeled 'Output'. The eye goes first to the fan-out between the two boxes.
caption: Illustration of the simplified one-layer transformer.
abstract: Large language models may encounter factual knowledge during pre-training yet fail to reliably use that knowledge after fine-tuning. We study this gap in a stylized one-layer self-attention + MLP transformer trained by next-token prediction and subsequently fine-tuned on question-answering data. We first prove that, under suitable regularity conditions, the model reaches near-optimal pre-training loss while learning structured attention patterns. We further show that fine-tuning turns the Q&A prompt format into a trigger for pre-trained relation features, enabling the model to extract facts not revisited during fine-tuning. Our analysis reveals a relation-covering characterization for knowledge extraction: fine-tuning need not revisit every stored fact, but it must cover enough latent relation-template directions through which facts were encoded during pre-training. We prove that extraction improves with pre-training multiplicity and fine-tuning coverage, but becomes harder as the relation-template universe grows. Conversely, insufficient coverage yields a failure regime in which facts can be stored but not extracted, providing a stylized mechanism for hallucination. Our analysis covers both full and low-rank fine-tuning, and experiments on synthetic data and PopQA-based GPT-2/Llama models support the predicted trends.
